artboards.title: 1 · Add a business, read its website
2 · What it sells: products and services
5 · Learn, one organisation at a time
6 · Team: roles, not a manager per project

annotations.text:
A NEW BUSINESS STARTS CLEAN

Innotrack is the example because you named it. The one line on the website is real: RFID Enabled Solutions for Mining & Asset Management.

That is all a plain read of the site returns, because the rest is drawn by script. DevDeck has to open the site in a browser window of its own to read the other pages. That is a real piece of work to build, not a detail.

Every suggestion says where it came from, and a guess says it is a guess.

PRODUCTS AND SERVICES

A product is something you build and it can have code. A service is work done for a customer, like an installation, with nothing to link.

The names here are examples built from the site's tagline, apart from Site surveys, shown as one you typed.

Mail read later in Learn can suggest more, and they come back to this list rather than being added quietly.

A PRODUCT HOLDS PROJECTS

Tick a repository and choose its product. It becomes a project in that product, cloned where you say, or used where it already is.

The repository names are made up.

GitHub sign-in in DevDeck is written but its app is not registered yet. Pasting a token works today, and that is enough to list repositories.

The website repository is offered to Marketing, not to a product.

MAIL

Same as before: every mailbox on the domain belongs to the business, and after the first only its address and password are asked for.

New here: a partner's own mailbox is theirs. It is only added if they share it.

LEARN, TIED TO WHAT IT SELLS

Each organisation is a client, supplier, adviser or partner firm, and says which products and services it has to do with. That is what lets the right role pick it up.

The organisations and facts are made up.

ROLES, THE WAY A COMPANY HAS THEM

One engineering lead for all three projects, one product manager for both products. A role owns work, never a folder, which is how the manager design in the roadmap already describes it.

The roles are suggested from what the business does. You put them on the team or keep doing them yourself, which shows as you do this rather than a gap.

Everyone reports to the directors. Reporting lines between roles can come later.

A manager already working for another business is offered above the roles, never assumed. Choosing it adds this business to its work instead of making a second one.

THE SPACE AFTERWARDS

Products hold their projects in the tree. Services and the organisation folders sit beside them.

The Team tab says what each role is on. Anything that needs a director, like a release or a dependency update, waits here and on Today, and nothing is pushed without a yes.

What each role is doing on this board is example content.
